rv.q: But with all its parts combined, this story from the city is something special: Dickens's late class drama turned into a work both elemental and righteous.
But this is still an ambitious, timely and compelling piece about the city, about society and about values — then and now.
But, much as I admired it, there's not enough drama or heart-leap to make this show a blockbuster.
Maybe the colour of Dickens's prose is lacking in Ian Rickson's efficient but sombre production.
...this story of poverty and class mobility is light on the satire and heavy on mood
It is not sufficiently wraparound-vibrant to achieve this.
Nonetheless, we emerge from this theatrical river feeling slightly soggy and mildly bewildered.
...impressionistic, swirling with ideas, but lacking a strong dramatic current.
A five-star wow bobbing in a three-star show.
With songs as flaccid commentary, this is a play with songs, not a musical.

“He do the police in different voices.” If ever one phrase summed up a work of fiction, and the art of its writer, then surely it is this description, by Charles Dickens in his 1865 novel, Our Mutual Friend, of his character Sloppy’s ability to read aloud from a newspaper.

On a stage which is pre-set to look like the backstage of any modern theatre, complete with lowered lighting-rig and blacked-out floors, the current production playing at the Lyttelton space, begins very much as it ends.
London Tide is flawed and grimy – but full of compelling promise.

It could be an episode of Silent Witness or the latest Scandi noir. London Tide, adapted from Charles Dickens’s novel Our Mutual Friend, opens with the discovery of a dead body in the river – but this grisly find is just another day at the office for waterman Gaffer Hexam, who makes his living from robbing water-logged corpses.
London Tide is eminently watchable, and if you don't already know its complex story, it has some real surprises.
They deserve better than to be drowned in the dour London Tide.
The show grinds on for more than three hours but there are a few highlights along the way.
But it is a sort of weird masterpiece and exactly what the NT should be doing.

cn.t: Critics split on this Dickens adaptation: some find it a striking stage thriller, while others dismiss it as undernourished and flat.
